text: Build a word dictionary class. Add word stores a word. Search returns true if any stored word matches it. The search word may contain dots, and a dot matches any letter.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a match means the whole word matches, not just a prefix. And a dot stands for exactly one letter. So b, dot, dot only matches three-letter words that start with b. Is that right?
Are there any constraints on the input size? And how many dots can one search have?
Words are one to twenty-five letters long. Lowercase letters, plus dots in search. At most two dots per search. At most ten to the fourth calls in total.

Okay. That dot limit is important — I'll come back to it when I talk about complexity. Let me run through the example. Add bad, dad, and mad. Then search pad is false — no word starts with p. Search bad is true. Search dot, a, d is true, because the dot can be b. Search b, dot, dot is true, because bad fits. So the output is null, null, null, null, false, true, true, true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to keep every word in a list. Then each search compares the pattern with every stored word, character by character, so the cost grows with the number of words stored. This problem reminds me of a prefix tree searched with depth-first backtracking. Words that share a start share one path, and a normal letter just follows one child. The new part is the dot. At a dot, I don't know which child to take, so I try all of them, and back up when a branch fails. That's a DFS over the trie.

Here's the plan. One: add word is a normal trie insert — create a child only when it's missing, then mark the end. Two: search runs a DFS with an index into the pattern and a node in the trie, moving down together. Three: in the DFS, a null node fails, the end of the pattern returns is-word, a letter follows one child, and a dot tries all twenty-six children and stops at the first true. One thing worth flagging — the null check at the top of the DFS does two jobs. It catches a letter with no child, like p in pad, and the many null children the dot loop passes in. Without it, the next line reads is-word from a null pointer — a correctness rule, not a style choice. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Add word is the same as a plain trie insert. Search just starts the DFS at the root. Inside the DFS, a letter makes one recursive call, and a dot makes up to twenty-six. The loop returns as soon as one branch finds a match. One thing worth flagging — inside the dot loop I write: if the DFS is true, return true. Not return the DFS directly. A bare return would give up after the very first child, so adding b and then searching dot would wrongly say false, because only child a was ever tried.
Good. Can you make it faster?

Follow-up: allocation dominates, so I'd use a node pool. Every new letter calls new TrieNode. Instead, I keep all nodes in one big array and use an int index as the pointer. Index zero is the root, so zero can also mean no child — the root is never anyone's child. Two small changes in the DFS. Letters are walked in a loop, so only a dot recurses. And I check the child before I recurse, so this version never calls the DFS on an empty slot. One thing worth flagging — this object is big, about twenty-five megabytes. It must live on the heap, not the stack. That's fine on LeetCode, because LeetCode creates it with new. And the array size comes from ten to the fourth words times twenty-five letters, plus the root, so it must be recomputed if the limits change.

Let's dry-run the code with the example. After the three adds, the trie has ten nodes, including the root. Expected: false, true, true, true. The row that matters is dot, a, d. The dot tries child a first, which is null, so the top check returns false and the loop moves on. Then it finds b, a, d and returns true right away, so dad and mad are never visited — five calls in total. That matches. Corner cases: dot, dot, x returns false after one hundred eight calls, and one hundred one of them land on null nodes — that's how much work the null check catches. And on an empty dictionary, any search returns false at the first null child instead of crashing.

Let me think about complexity here. Add word is linear in L, the word length, and a search with no dots is also linear. With k dots, each dot can branch twenty-six ways, so the worst case is twenty-six to the k, times L. Here the limit is two dots, so at most six hundred seventy-six branches. That's why the dot limit matters — it keeps search small. Space is total added characters times twenty-six pointers for the trie, plus linear recursion depth for the DFS. The node pool has the same Big-O; the win is the constant. On a LeetCode-like workload, the pointer version took about one hundred sixty-seven milliseconds, and the pool about thirty-three. There's a trade-off here: the pool reserves about twenty-five megabytes up front, even for a few words.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw that only search changes: a dot means try every child. You explained that the single null check at the top of the DFS covers both missing letters and the null children from the dot loop. And you tied the complexity to the two-dot limit, so twenty-six to the k stays small. The node pool follow-up was a nice touch, and you backed it with numbers. Good work.
